# AI & Labor Markets Papers — 2026-11-25

## 1. AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand [Firm Adoption]

**Authors:** Lindsey Raymond, Eleanor Wiske Dillon
**Date:** first posted 2026-11-23
**Source:** arXiv:2611.31083
**Summary:** The authors study firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce, using a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles to identify causal effects. One year after adoption, Copilot reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration, and the hiring slowdown is concentrated in junior technical roles with the highest share of routine coding work. The paper offers some of the first firm-level causal evidence that AI coding assistance shifts labor demand toward more experienced workers and hybrid coding/design roles rather than shrinking headcount outright.

## 2. How AI Impacts Skill Formation [Skills & Tasks]

**Authors:** Judy Hanwen Shen, Alex Tamkin
**Date:** first posted 2026-01-28; revised 2026-11-23
**Source:** arXiv:2601.20245
**Summary:** Using randomized experiments, the authors study how developers learn a new asynchronous programming library with and without AI assistance, finding that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging ability without delivering significant average efficiency gains. Workers who fully delegated tasks to AI showed some productivity improvement but learned the least, while the authors identify distinct AI-interaction patterns, some of which preserve learning even with AI help. The findings bear on human-capital formation under AI assistance, suggesting that AI-driven productivity gains for novice workers can come at the cost of the skill acquisition firms and workers need for long-run productivity.

## Excluded, borderline

- **When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews** (Alsayed; arXiv:2611.28426) — on-topic subject (automated interview scoring) but a methods paper evaluated on 540 synthetic interview responses against AI-generated provisional references; it produces no finding about real hiring, wage, or worker outcomes.
- **Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems** (Roy, Majumdar & Deb; arXiv:2611.20140) — on-topic (LLM resume screening) but an audit of system architecture, operational accuracy, and compliance/security properties of the screening tool itself, not of any labor-market or candidate outcome.
- **Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy** (Das, Leduc & Guha; arXiv:2611.19111) — relevant theme (skills and AI policy) but relies on 3,200 simulated generative agents rating hypothetical policies, not observed labor-market behavior or outcomes.
- **Has AI Widened Employment Gaps? Tracking Early-Career Employment by Occupational Exposure in Norway** (Hernaes & Kostøl; IZA DP 18767) — directly on-topic (early-career employment by AI exposure) but dated June 2026 with no listed revision, outside the 30-day window.
- **AI, Output, and Employment** (Johnston & Makridis; CESifo WP 12579) and **Automation in the Wake of GenAI** (Gschwendt & Schilter; Zurich Economics of Education WP 0252) — both on-topic (AI exposure/output/employment; entry-level training cuts) but both trace to early-to-mid-2026 NEP announcement dates, outside the window.
- **Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market** (arXiv:2610.14850) — on-topic agent-based search-and-matching model of AI displacement, but published and updated 2026-10-10, outside the 30-day window.

## Sourcing note

Both NBER RSS feeds were unreachable (`nber.org/papers.rss` and `nber.org/programs/ls/papers.rss` both 301-redirect to non-feed HTML pages), consistent with recent digests, so coverage relied on the arXiv API plus a budgeted IZA/CEPR/RePEc web search. All non-arXiv candidates found in the supplement search traced to publication dates well outside the 30-day window.
